You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

Actually the typical pattern: count occurrences of each color; colors appearing once (singletons) are noise to be removed; keep regions of the dominant color per area. But there are pairs like 3 appearing multiple times... The known task: remove all "singular" cells (colors that appear exactly once), replacing with the most common color of their surrounding region? Hmm.

Actually known ARC task: the scattered unique-colored pixels get deleted (set to surrounding region color), and the answer grid is just the three regions cleaned. Singleton 7 at (9,10) within 7 region.

Perhaps the rule: pixels colored 2,3,5,9 etc are noise; the real structure is regions 8, 7, 4. Noise cells become the region's color? But 3s: e.g. (27,11) inside 4-block, (15,3) in 8-region. If we replace noise with surrounding color, output = grid with only 8,7,4 regions cleaned.

But maybe the rule: count colors; each non-background color appears exactly N times... maybe noise colors (2,3,5,9) form a pattern — dots scattered. Alternative known task: each noise color appears once per region, and the answer moves them? This could be the "count dots, draw rectangle" family... Hard.

Best to request a demo to check. Cost analysis: asking for 1 demo costs 1; wrong submissions cost 1 each; unsolved = 16. With 8 demos and 8 attempts, a demo is cheap insurance. Get one demo pair, infer rule, submit.

Scattered noise colors 2,3,5,9 across an 8 background and 7 region and 4 block. Simplest hypothesis: output removes all noise cells, replacing with surrounding region color (8 mostly, 7 in the 7 region, 4 in the 4 block). Note noise inside 7 region: 2 at (4,6) and 3 at (1,7) — inside 7 region; 2 at (15,11) inside 7 region. Noise in 4 block: 3 at (27,11).

But which color should a noise cell become? Likely the region color (most common neighbor). But maybe there's more: noise dots might be counted and something drawn. Cost-wise, safest guess: replace noise with local region color. But guessing wrong costs 1 each, up to 8 attempts. Alternative: get a demo to confirm — costs 1 and reduces risk. I'll request one demo first.

Demo confirms: noise cells (8s,3s,7s scattered) replaced with the region color they sit in. Note demo noise colors were also region colors (6,2,1) plus noise 8,3,7 — removed. So replace each cell not belonging to a solid region with the dominant color of its region.

Test: regions 8 (big), 7 (rectangle rows 0-15 cols 4-9? plus rows 9-15 cols 10-12), 4 block rows 25-27 cols 8-12. Determine region color per noise cell via nearest dominant. Simpler: region = connected component of majority colors; noise cell takes the color of surrounding region. Do BFS: assign each noise cell to nearest region cell's color (8/7/4).

Let me implement: identify "solid" colors = colors forming large connected blocks (8,7,4). Then flood-fill regions of solid colors. Noise cells take color of any adjacent region cell, iteratively.
